blocks: Keep the forearms together and raise them as high as you can through a full range, then lower them. The set ends when the elbows separate.
The video does two sets of 10 to 15 lifts. If full repetitions are too hard, press up once and hold the squeeze.
Squeeze each finger, the palms, and the elbows together the whole time; the exercise stops working when the elbows come apart.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's elbow-squeeze arm raise, 10:00. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice a long-spine hip hinge with a comfortable arm reach and steady breathing.
Stand with feet a little wider than shoulder width and knees softly bent. Hinge at the hips so the hips move backward and the torso inclines forward.
Lengthen through the spine, lift the chest, and raise the arms only as far as you can while keeping the position comfortable. Breathe and exhale slowly, then return to standing.
Begin with a shallow hinge and a few calm breaths, then stand to reset. Add reach or hinge depth gradually while keeping the spine controlled.
Begin with a shallow hinge and a few slow breaths. Keep the arms lower if raising them makes the back arch or the shoulders uncomfortable.
Demonstration: Huberman's Founder pose, 5:15. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's founder, 0:00. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice loading the femur into the hip socket on hands and knees to restore internal and external hip rotation.
Kneel on all fours with the working knee under the hip at 90 degrees of hip flexion. Draw the knee toward the midline to wind up the hip capsule.

Push your weight back through the femur toward the back of the hip, then glide sideways without dropping to the ground, keeping that line of force. From there add a little more flexion or rotation, move the pelvis and torso on the femur, or use the other leg to press the working leg into internal or external rotation.
About two minutes per side, per the video. Assess rotation before and after.

Aim for a rotation window of 75 to 90 degrees with the femur vertical and loaded, about 45 degrees external and 30 degrees internal. If the front of the hip pinches, loop a band around the upper thigh and anchor it to the side or behind you to pull the femur slightly out of the socket.
Demonstration: Kelly Starrett's joint capsule mobilization, 5:30. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/20/05/If Your Hip Doesn't Rotate You Can't Be at Full Power.
Practice a controlled hip-extension position that stretches the front of the rear hip.
In a split stance or half-kneeling lunge, place one leg behind the body and keep the pelvis facing forward. Use support for balance or padding under the rear knee.

Gently move the pelvis forward while keeping the trunk tall and the low back comfortable. Aim for a stretch at the front of the rear hip. Raising the same-side arm can add to the movement, provided the back remains controlled.
Begin with 10–30 seconds per side and repeat as comfortable. Add range gradually while keeping the low back comfortable.
Begin with 10–30 seconds per side and repeat as comfortable. A shorter stance and smaller movement are useful starting versions. Avoid creating the stretch only by arching the lower back.
Demonstration: Huberman's hip-extension stretch, 2:15. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's lunge stretch, 2:37. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice moving into a supported shoulder-extension position while raising the hips.
Sit with knees bent, feet flat, and hands behind the hips, fingers pointing outward. Press through hands and feet to raise the hips toward a tabletop position.
Keep the neck comfortable and breathe. Lift only as high as your shoulders and wrists comfortably allow; begin with short holds and lower under control.
Begin with short holds and work toward a comfortable ten-second hold. Increase height or try the next shoulder-extension variation only while the position remains comfortable.
Work toward a comfortable ten-second hold before trying the video's further shoulder-extension progressions. Keep a lower hip position or a shorter hold if full height is not comfortable.
Demonstration: Huberman's reverse tabletop, 3:41. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Practice upper-body rotation while maintaining a comfortable wide squat.
Take a wide stance with toes turned slightly outward. Lower into a comfortable squat with the feet grounded, then place the elbows lightly against the inner knees.

Keep one elbow supported while raising the other arm and turning the upper body to follow the hand with the eyes. Return to the center and change sides. Point diagonally upward if reaching the ceiling is uncomfortable.
Begin with three slow turns per side, pausing briefly and breathing. Add range gradually while keeping the squat stable.
Start with three slow turns per side, pausing briefly and breathing. Use a shallower squat or hold a stable support when the bottom position is difficult.
Demonstration: Huberman's sumo squat with rotation, 0:28. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Practice a split-stance hip hinge that loads the front glute and hamstring while the back stays braced.
Stand with one foot forward and one back, feet pointing the same way and hips square. Bend the front knee slightly and keep it behind the ankle.

Brace the spine, push the hips back, and press the chest forward until the front hamstring stretches. Reach the arms forward and up and hold. Then cross the arms over the chest and hinge up and down, moving the upper body as one unit from the front hip.
The video holds the reach briefly, adds a rotation toward the front leg as 10 to 15 repetitions or a static hold, then does 8 to 10 hinges per side.
Press through the front heel and keep the front knee from sliding forward. Any bend in the lower back means the hinge has gone too far.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's split-stance hinge, 3:31. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice lowering and raising the torso from a hip-hinged position on a hyperextension bench to train the lower back and hip extensors.

Adjust a hyperextension (45-degree or horizontal) bench so the pad sits just below the hip crease and the heels are secured under the ankle rollers. Start with the body in a straight line, hands crossed on the chest or behind the head.

Bend at the hips to lower the torso slowly toward the floor, then raise it back until the body is in a straight line again. Stop at a straight line rather than arching the lower back past it. Each repetition is slow and controlled.
Huberman suggests 8 to 25 controlled repetitions per set and does about 100 repetitions a week. Add load by holding a plate or dumbbell at the chest or by anchoring a band under the bench.

Reduce the range or remove the added load if the movement turns into a swing or the lower back pinches at the top. Without a machine, hold the edge of a high countertop or sturdy table with the torso supported and lift the legs behind you.
Demonstration: Huberman's back hyperextension, 9:53. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles.
Practice a loaded squat that develops leg strength while maintaining a stable trunk.

Set the rack hooks just below shoulder height and the safety bars below the bottom of your squat. Center the bar across the upper back, grip it securely, stand to unrack it, and take a short step back.

Brace your trunk, keep the whole foot planted, and bend hips and knees together. Lower through the deepest comfortable range you can control, then push the floor away to stand. Let your knees track in the direction of your toes.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.
Reduce the load or depth if your heels lift or your trunk position changes abruptly. A light goblet squat is a way to practice the pattern; the leg press below is a machine alternative.
Demonstration: Huberman's back squat, 0:27. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 2 - Major Lower Body Muscles.
Practice a horizontal barbell press with a repeatable grip, stable support, and controlled bar path.

Set the bench and rack so you can unrack without reaching excessively. Use rack safeties or a capable spotter. Lie with feet planted, shoulders supported, and hands slightly wider than shoulder width; wrap the thumbs around the bar.
Lower the bar slowly toward the chest while keeping wrists stacked over forearms, then press upward. Keep the hips on the bench and avoid bouncing the bar off the chest.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.
A machine chest press is a substitute when a suitable rack or spotter is unavailable. Start with a light bar to establish a repeatable grip and bar path.
Demonstration: Huberman's bench press, 0:07. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles. Additional instructions: ACE's barbell chest press.
Practice a squat with the load hung from a hip belt, training the legs without loading the spine or shoulders.

Use a belt-squat machine, or a dip belt with a plate hanging between the feet while you stand on two raised boxes. Fasten the belt around the hips and hold the machine's handles or a support for balance.
Stand tall, then bend hips and knees together to lower the load under control. Keep the torso upright and the whole foot planted. Push the floor away to stand.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.
Huberman likes this compound option, though most gyms don't have the machine. It suits days when the back or shoulders limit the Exercise/Body/Strength/Back Squat.
Demonstration: Huberman's other compound options, 4:54. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 2 - Major Lower Body Muscles.
Practice elbow flexion against resistance with a steady upper arm and controlled wrist.
Stand or sit with a dumbbell in each hand, arms down, and trunk steady. Curl by bending the elbows; turn the palms upward if comfortable, then lower slowly.
Keep the upper arms mostly still and the wrists aligned with the forearms. Reduce the load if you must swing the torso or move the elbows far forward to finish.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.
A seated curl or cable curl can make the starting position easier to repeat. An EZ-bar is another grip option.
Demonstration: Huberman's curl, 4:44. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 7 - Shoulders and Arms.
Practice a chest isolation movement against cables, which keep resistance on the chest through the whole range.
Set two cable pulleys slightly above shoulder height. Take a handle in each hand, step forward into a staggered stance, and let the arms open out to the sides with a slight bend in the elbows.
Keeping the elbow bend fixed, draw the hands together in front of the chest. Pause for a second, then let the arms open slowly back to the start.
Huberman suggests two to three work sets of 6 to 15 repetitions. Add resistance only while the elbow angle and stance stay steady.

Reduce the load if you lean or step to finish a repetition. Moving the pulleys higher or lower changes the line of pull toward the lower or upper chest. A seated fly machine (pec deck) uses the same pattern with a fixed path and back support.
Demonstration: Huberman's cable fly, 4:51. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles. Additional instructions: ACE's standing chest fly.
Practice a horizontal pull while a pad or bench supports the torso.

On a rowing machine, adjust the chest pad so you can reach the handles with extended arms while the chest remains supported. Set the seat so the handle path is comfortable and the feet stay supported.
Brace, row the handles toward your ribs, pause, and extend the arms slowly. Keep your chest in contact with the pad instead of lifting away to finish a repetition.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.
For dumbbells, use an incline bench that supports the chest while leaving space for the arms to hang and row. Begin light; a different bench angle changes both the clearance and the line of pull.
Source for the supported machine version: ACE's seated row with chest pad.
Practice pulling the chin straight back to activate the deep neck flexors that forward head posture weakens.
Sit, stand, or lie with the head level and the eyes looking straight ahead.
Draw the chin straight back without tipping the head up or down. If needed, place an index finger on the point of the chin and push it straight in. Hold, then release.
Repetitions and holds follow the training plan. Once the tuck is strong, hold it through each direction of the Exercise/Body/Strength/Plate Neck Raise.
The movement is straight back, not down toward the chest. Rounded shoulders pull the head forward and up, stretching and weakening the front of the neck; the tuck counters that.
Demonstration: Jeff Cavaliere's chin tuck, 5:07. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/16/11/Neck Exercises that Kill Your Neck.
Practice hand-grip strength by squeezing a spring barbell collar, then flexing and extending the wrist while holding partial tension.
Hold a spring barbell collar in one hand as you would a hand gripper.

Squeeze the collar closed and release it until failure. Then hold it with a little tension and move the wrist back into extension and down into flexion, keeping the grip, until you can no longer control it.
Sets and repetitions follow the training plan. The video runs it as a drop-set burnout on each hand, with a Exercise/Body/Strength/Farmer's Carry between sets.
Holding tension with the wrist flexed is hard because the finger flexors are already shortened; that is the part being trained. A hand gripper can replace the collar.
Demonstration: Jeff Cavaliere's collar grip combo, 11:10. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/18/12/The Perfect Forearm Workout.
Practice hanging from a bar with straight arms for as long as possible to build grip endurance.
Grip a pull-up bar overhand about shoulder width apart and lift the feet so the body hangs with the arms straight.
Hold the hang with a firm grip, keeping the bar in the palms. End the set when the grip fails, then step down.
Duration follows the training plan. Jeff Cavaliere gives 1:40 as an average fresh hang; at the end of his forearm workout he aims for one more minute.
Squeeze hard and keep the bar from sliding into the fingers, which loads the inner elbow. Feet on a box for partial support is an easier version.
Demonstration: Jeff Cavaliere's dead arm hang, 12:44. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/18/12/The Perfect Forearm Workout.
Practice lifting a barbell from the floor with a hip hinge, training the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back along with grip and trunk strength.

Stand with feet about hip to shoulder width apart and the bar over the middle of the feet, close to the shins. Hinge and bend the knees to grip the bar just outside the legs with an overhand grip. Flatten the back and lift the chest.

Brace, then push the feet into the floor and drive the hips forward to stand tall, keeping the bar close to the legs. Think of hinging instead of yanking the bar upward. Lower it by pushing the hips back and bending the knees once the bar passes them, and keep the back flat until the bar touches the floor.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.

Grip often gives out before the legs; an over-under grip, with one palm up, is a common way to hold heavier loads. The glutes and hamstrings should do the work, not the lower back. The Exercise/Body/Strength/Trap-Bar Deadlift uses neutral handles beside the body; the Exercise/Body/Strength/Romanian Deadlift starts standing and keeps the knees nearly straight.
Demonstration: Huberman's deadlift, 6:18. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 2 - Major Lower Body Muscles. Source: ACE's deadlift.
Practice lowering and pressing the body between parallel bars to train the chest, front and side shoulders, and triceps.
Grip parallel bars, jump or step up, and support yourself with straight arms and the shoulders pulled down away from the ears.

Lean the torso forward somewhat and bend the elbows to lower the body under control until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor or to the deepest point you control without shoulder pain. Press back up to straight arms. Keep the shoulder blades set back and down so the shoulders do not roll forward at the bottom.

Sets, repetitions, and rest follow the training plan. Once 10 to 15 bodyweight repetitions come easily, add load, for example a dumbbell held between the feet or a dip belt. Huberman calls the weighted dip an upper body squat.

A more forward lean emphasizes the chest; a more upright torso shifts work toward the triceps. Use an assisted dip machine or a band for support until full bodyweight repetitions are possible. Stop the set if the front of the shoulder hurts at the bottom.
Demonstration: Huberman's dips, 3:15. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles.
Practice a horizontal press with a dumbbell in each hand, which lets each arm work on its own path and allows the weights to be set aside if a repetition fails.

Sit on the end of a flat bench with the dumbbells standing on your knees. Lean back and kick them up one knee at a time so they arrive at the shoulders as your back reaches the bench. Plant the feet, pull the shoulder blades down and back, and keep head, shoulders, and hips on the bench.

Press the dumbbells up until the elbows are straight, with wrists stacked over the elbows. Lower slowly toward the middle of the chest, slightly wide toward the armpits, then press back up without arching the lower back. At the end of the set, bring the weights back to the chest and sit up with them on the knees, or hand them to a spotter.

Sets, repetitions, resistance, and rest follow the training plan. Establish a repeatable movement with a light load first; add resistance gradually after completing the planned repetitions with consistent control.

If a repetition fails, lower the dumbbells to the sides and drop them clear of the body rather than straining to finish. Getting into and out of position safely limits the usable load more than the press itself; practice the kick-up with a light pair. Keeping the elbows closer to the sides shifts work toward the triceps; flaring them shifts it toward the chest.

Demonstration: Huberman's dumbbell bench press, 1:08. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles. Additional instructions: ACE's dumbbell chest press.
Practice an arcing chest isolation movement with dumbbells and a fixed bend in the elbows.

Lie on a flat or slightly inclined bench with a dumbbell in each hand, feet planted and shoulder blades pulled down and back. Hold the weights above the chest, palms facing each other, elbows slightly bent.

Keeping the elbow bend fixed, lower the dumbbells in a wide arc until the upper arms reach about chest level or a comfortable stretch. Bring them back up along the same arc, as if hugging a large barrel.
Huberman suggests two to three work sets of 6 to 15 repetitions. Add load only while the elbow angle stays fixed.

If the elbows bend more as the weights come down, the fly has turned into a press; use lighter dumbbells. Huberman demonstrates a slight incline. At the end of a set, bring the weights together over the chest and sit up before setting them down rather than straining to lower them to the floor from the bottom position. A Exercise/Body/Strength/Cable Fly keeps tension through the whole movement.
Demonstration: Huberman's dumbbell fly, 4:20. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles. Additional instructions: ACE's lying chest fly.
Practice pressing a pair of dumbbells from shoulder height overhead while each arm balances its own load.

Lift the dumbbells off the floor with bent knees and a flat back, as in a deadlift, then bring them to the shoulders. Sit on a flat bench or a bench with back support, plant the feet, and brace the trunk.
Press both dumbbells overhead, then lower them under control to shoulder height. Keep the forearms underneath the dumbbells and the ribs over the pelvis.
